story_text.value:
I'm currently a CS student, so that means a lot of file uploads to my university's janky website. I hated having to sort through the file picker just to attach an assignment open the next tab over. Pasteup is a Chrome extension that lets you press Cmd+V / Ctrl+V on the page instead, it finds the corresponding file box and attaches them automatically (if there are multiple it opens a picker).

Moreover I added an automatic file converter, so for things like CSV, txt, and code, it automatically converts it to the right format. This means my workflow went from going to the assignment sorting through 15 finder folders and uploading to ctrl a ctrl c ctrl v.

The file converter is pretty smart, and supports a lot of formats. If the field only takes PDF or JPG, it converts the file before uploading. It also turns copied spreadsheet cells into a CSV, JSON into a .json, and Figma's "Copy as SVG" into an image.

If you're already in any text boxes or editors it does nothing. If the site handles paste itself (FilePond, chat apps), it goes first, and Pasteup does nothing.

It runs entirely locally: no servers, no analytics, no network requests, no third-party libraries.

I'd love to hear about sites where it picks the wrong field or gets in the way or just any feedback in general!

story_text.value:
I've been working on this project for a few years, and thinking about it for a few more years. Ever since the pandemic when I did my entire job on a little Chromebook with browser-based tools; why not make an Audacity for the browser?

Well, it turned out there were already a few "Audacities for the Browser" like https://audiomass.co/ (posted here a couple times already), https://naomiaro.com/waveform-playlist/, and a literal Audacity compiled to WebAssembly https://wavacity.com/. SoundEtch is kind of a beefed up version of those.

I made it with podcasters and other spoken-word creators in mind, rather than musicians, since there are a number of browser DAWs already e.g. OpenDAW.

Everything is streamed to and from disk (OPFS), with an optional cloud backup. You can close or crash the browser tab, even in the middle of recording, and your data is still there when you open it back up. This also means you can load huge files; my parents' desktop with 8gb RAM handled this 5 hour stereo mp3 I found on archive https://archive.org/details/2023-09-08/2023-09-10.mp3.

There's a transcription-based editing tool like you get with Riverside and Descript. Mine uses IBM's Granite Turbo model, plus some Codex/Claude tweaking to get word-level timestamps. The result is, to my knowledge, much faster and more accurate than any other browser/local ASR out there. It has a few quirks, though, like only emitting lower-case letters and spaces.

I also added a WebRTC meeting room with up to 4 guests. It doesn't have a TURN service, so some networks will block you from connecting.

Since AI coding assistants are so good these days, I was able to add video support pretty easily. You can import, export, and record video, add that transcript with the current word highlighted, etc.

The editing is pretty basic for now: you can trim the clips, move them around, add some effects including noise removal from DeepFilterNet (https://github.com/Rikorose/DeepFilterNet).

I appreciate your taking a look and any feedback you have! The code is at https://github.com/bfbsoundetch/SoundEtch

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

I've always been a big fan of the Civ games, and was always frustrated at how terrible the AI was. So I got curious about whether LLMs could play Civ well, or not! I thought about having the agents interact with the GUI directly, but something about that seemed like the wrong approach. For one thing, it seemed to me like images would cost way more in tokens. For another, LLMs seem like a different kind of intelligence from humans, so why would an interface meant for humans be optimal for them?

Anyway, I spend a few weeks modifying Unciv [0], an open-source reimplementation of Civ V to have the right endpoints and views for an agent to be able to play civ in the same way a person could. You can see the first game running at the link. So far, it looks like the GPT models are able to play a reasonable game - definitely better than the built-in AI, which was my barometer for success! You can find the harness here: https://github.com/varchasgopalaswamy/unciv-ai. Let me know what you folks think!

[0]: https://github.com/yairm210/Unciv

story_text.value:
Here is a fun project if you want to make an open-source Meta Muse Charm.

It is a cheap ESP32-S3 talking toy from Shanghai talking to my Mac/Linux desktop app (BoBe), with zero API keys on the chip. I mapped the screen, audio and power-latch pins with no schematic, and wired a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 to press its physical buttons automatically behind a packet-loss router to test bad Wi-Fi.

Not selling anything, just a hobby project, all is free and open source on GitHub, if you find it interesting feel free to use it: https://johnkozaris.com/blog/bobe-toy-robot-body

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I built a mutation testing tool that takes a different approach from the conventional one. I'm calling it Targeted Mutation Testing.

As AI coding has become more common, mutation testing has become more important. It has helped me a lot personally. But ever since I first learned about it, I've kept wondering if there was a smarter way to do it.

Targeted Mutation Testing observes a single test run and generates targeted mutants from what it sees.

Of course, observation-guided rules have their own limits, so you can also combine them with classic mutation rules when you want more coverage.

This post links to the Rust implementation, which I built first. I also built a JS/TS implementation:

https://github.com/t-k/targeted-mutation-ts

What's interesting about the JS/TS version is that, by focusing on targeted mutants, mutation testing can become practical for E2E tests.

I took inspiration from SEMu, DSpot, the W-method, and Meta's ACH. I listed the links at the end.

Would love any feedback. Thanks for taking a look.

- Killing Stubborn Mutants with Symbolic Execution (SEMu): https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02941

- Automatic Test Improvement with DSpot: https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.08330

- Testing Software Design Modeled by Finite-State Machines (W-method): https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.1978.231496

- Mutation-Guided LLM-based Test Generation at Meta (ACH): https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12862

story_text.value:
a ball will fall. trade on where it lands.

I made this game! Some technical details:

The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome.

There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky.

Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.
